strengths: Conceptual novelty: Adapting Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) to discretized time series provides an elegant, variable-length, pattern-centric tokenization scheme that directly addresses the rigidity of fixed-length patching and the inefficiency of point-wise tokenization.

Conditional decoding formulation: The proposed conditional dequantization step is closed-form, computationally negligible at inference time, and provides consistent error reductions across multiple tokenizers and datasets.

Extensive foundation model training and empirical evaluation: The authors trained 31 T5 models up to 710M parameters on the large-scale Chronos dataset (11B samples) and systematically benchmarked against strong foundation model baselines (Chronos, MOMENT, MOIRAI).

Thorough ablation and interpretability analysis: The manuscript includes detailed investigations of vocabulary size, occurrence thresholds ($p_{\min}$), quantization granularity, dataset size scaling, and PCA explainability showing that the learned embeddings capture statistical moments, trends, and parent-child hierarchical relations.
weaknesses: Historical context length discrepancy: The experiments fix the context length to 128 tokens for both Chronos and the proposed motif-based models. Because motif tokens compress several time steps (average compression $\bar{c} \in [2.08, 4.06]$ and higher on Weather), the proposed model effectively receives substantially longer raw historical context than Chronos (e.g., 250 to 500+ time steps vs. exactly 128 steps). Chronos should also be evaluated with comparable historical sample lengths to isolate the benefit of motif representation from the benefit of longer lookback windows.

Zero-shot protocol ambiguity in conditional decoding: In Section 5.3, the text states that conditional decoding is trained on the respective target dataset's training split and evaluated on the test set. Calibrating decoding parameters on the target domain deviates from a strict zero-shot setting and gives an advantage over pure zero-shot foundation model baselines. While Appendix C.3 evaluates a model-independent version trained on Chronos, the main text should clearly distinguish between in-domain calibrated and strictly zero-shot decoding.

Evaluation metrics: Results are reported exclusively in terms of point MSE. Since the baseline Chronos model is designed for probabilistic forecasting and standard time series benchmarks evaluate both MAE and probabilistic metrics (e.g., CRPS / WQL), reporting these metrics would provide a more complete assessment.

Handling of forecast horizon boundaries: Autoregressive motif generation outputs variable-length segments per step. The manuscript does not clearly describe how truncation or stopping is handled when generating a fixed-length horizon (e.g., exactly 64 steps) if the final predicted motif exceeds the target boundary.

strengths: Novel and intuitive formulation: Adapting Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) to discretized time series allows the model to naturally capture recurring temporal motifs of variable lengths, effectively bridging the gap between inefficient single-sample tokenization (e.g., Chronos) and rigid fixed-length patch representations.

Compelling efficiency-accuracy trade-offs: The proposed motif-based representation significantly compresses sequence lengths, leading to substantial inference speedups (up to 56x) while consistently matching or improving forecasting MSE compared to standard Chronos models.

Clever, lightweight conditional decoding: The proposed post-hoc conditional dequantization analytically solves for the optimal reconstruction values based on consecutive symbol transitions without requiring gradient optimization or backpropagation, yielding substantial error reductions practically for free.

Thorough empirical analysis and interpretability: The paper provides extensive ablations on quantization bins, frequency thresholds, vocabulary size, and tokenizer training set size, accompanied by compelling representational analyses (PCA) illustrating how embeddings structure statistical moments (mean, variance), trends, and parent-child hierarchy.
weaknesses: Ambiguity in autoregressive generation for fixed horizons: Because motifs have variable lengths, autoregressively predicting tokens will rarely match the exact target forecast horizon (e.g., exactly 64 time steps) without overshoot. The manuscript lacks explicit discussion in the main text on how motif boundaries, truncation, or overshoot are handled during sequence generation.

In-domain training of conditional decoding: In Section 5.3, conditional decoding parameters are fitted on the training split of each target evaluation dataset before testing. While post-hoc and lightweight, this introduces target-domain supervision/calibration into an otherwise zero-shot evaluation protocol. Clarifying the performance gap between purely zero-shot conditional decoding (as in Table 10) and target-tuned conditional decoding in the main tables would make the claims more rigorous.

Evaluation dataset breadth: While the 5 benchmark datasets (ETT, Weather, Electricity, Traffic) are standard in the time-series literature, evaluating on a broader subset of the Monash repository or the full Chronos evaluation suite would better substantiate claims regarding universal foundation model generalization.

strengths: Novel and conceptually elegant application of Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) to time series: discretizing continuous series into uniform bins and recursively merging frequent pairs into a motif vocabulary directly tackles the token-inefficiency of point-wise autoregressive models like Chronos.

Conditional decoding offers a computationally virtually free (closed-form bigram expected-value lookup table) post-processing method to mitigate quantization error without gradient updates or inference latency overhead.
Extensive empirical execution involving substantial compute: pre-training 31 T5 foundation models ranging from 8M to 710M parameters across varying vocabulary sizes and compression ratios.

Thorough explainability and analytical evaluations, including PCA of token embeddings demonstrating natural separation of mean, standard deviation, and trends, alongside analyses of parent-child embedding proximity and token occurrence thresholds.
weaknesses: Confounded context length comparison: The paper sets the context window to 128 tokens for both Chronos and the proposed motif models. However, because motif tokens represent compressed sequences (average compression factor c_bar between 2x and 23x), the proposed model is effectively provided with a much longer historical context in raw time steps (e.g., 260 to 500+ steps, and even more on Weather) compared to Chronos (strictly 128 steps). It is unclear whether the reported MSE gains stem from the motif inductive bias or simply from observing a significantly larger historical window.

Questionable zero-shot protocol for conditional decoding: In Section 5.3, the authors state that conditional decoding parameters are fitted on the target dataset's training split before evaluating on the test split. Using target dataset data violates strict zero-shot evaluation protocols and gives an unfair advantage over zero-shot baselines that do not access target training splits.

Lack of clarification on variable-length autoregressive termination: Standard forecasting requires predicting an exact fixed horizon H (e.g., 64 steps). Since motifs span variable lengths, autoregressively generating motif tokens can overshoot or undershoot the desired horizon. The paper does not specify the boundary condition, stopping criterion, or how partial motif completions are decoded.

Mixed results against competitive patch-based baselines: While the method outperforms MOMENT, it lags behind Morai on 3 out of 5 benchmark datasets in Table 3 (Weather, Electricity, and Traffic), showing that fixed-length patching with continuous embeddings remains highly competitive.

Limited evaluation benchmark suite: Evaluating zero-shot foundation models on only five standard benchmark datasets (ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather, Electricity, Traffic) is limited compared to contemporary time-series foundation model literature, which typically benchmarks on extensive collections such as the Monash archive or LOTSA.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated concept: Adapting Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) to discretized time series addresses a key limitation in current time series foundation models—namely, the trade-off between computationally inefficient point-wise tokenization (e.g., Chronos) and rigid, fixed-length patching.

Rigorous and controlled experimental setup: The isolated comparison against Chronos ensures that architecture (T5), pretraining data, and training budgets are matched, isolating the impact of the tokenization scheme itself. The method demonstrates strong Pareto improvements across accuracy (MSE) and inference speed.

Lightweight and effective conditional decoding: The proposed analytical conditional decoding is closed-form, gradient-free, adds negligible inference cost, and significantly mitigates quantization error.

Comprehensive empirical analysis and interpretability: The paper includes extensive ablations (e.g., quantization bins, motif frequency threshold, dataset scaling) and insightful representation analyses (PCA of motif embeddings capturing mean, variance, and trend; parent-child embedding similarity; and robustness against noise, trends, and transients).
weaknesses: Nuance regarding zero-shot evaluation with Conditional Decoding: In Section 5.3 and Table 2, conditional decoding is calibrated on the training split of the evaluation dataset before predicting the test split. While computationally trivial (an $M \times M$ lookup table of sample means), this technically breaks the strictly zero-shot paradigm for the results reported in the main tables. Although Appendix C.3 explores a dataset-independent version trained purely on Chronos data, the distinction between strictly zero-shot and train-split-calibrated decoding should be clarified upfront in the main paper.

Handling fixed forecast horizons during variable-length autoregressive generation: Because motifs have variable sample lengths, autoregressively generating tokens does not naturally align with a fixed forecast horizon (e.g., exactly 64 steps). The manuscript would benefit from clarifying how generation termination, over-generation, and truncation are handled during evaluation.

Evaluation dataset breadth: While the 5 benchmark datasets (ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather, Electricity, Traffic) are standard in the literature, recent time series foundation models are frequently evaluated across broader benchmark collections (e.g., Monash archive or GIFT-Eval). Broadening the zero-shot suite would further validate generalization across diverse domains.

strengths: Novel and elegant adaptation of Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) to time series: While BPE is standard in NLP, applying it hierarchically to uniformly quantized 1D temporal series provides a natural way to achieve adaptive, variable-length pattern compression.

Conditional decoding is an effective, lightweight technique: Using an analytical first-order Markov dequantization conditioned on the previous point introduces zero gradient overhead, very few parameters ($M^2$), and substantially reduces discretization error (up to 44% MSE reduction).

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The authors train multiple model sizes (tiny to large, up to 710M parameters) on massive datasets (Chronos pretraining corpus) and evaluate across 5 benchmark datasets in a zero-shot setting, demonstrating Pareto improvements in inference speed (up to 26x-56x acceleration) and forecasting accuracy over sample-wise Chronos.

Rich qualitative and representational analyses: The PCA embeddings clearly capture fundamental time series properties (mean, variance, linear/quadratic trends, motif length), and extensive ablations explore vocabulary depth, noise robustness, non-stationarity, and transient outliers.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation horizon: The zero-shot evaluation is conducted primarily on a single prediction horizon of 64 steps. Standard long-term time series forecasting benchmarks typically test across multiple horizons (e.g., 96, 192, 336, 720 steps); demonstrating performance across diverse prediction horizons would strengthen the empirical claims.

Horizon boundary handling during autoregressive generation: Because motifs have variable lengths, generating an exact prediction horizon (e.g., exactly 64 steps) requires handling boundary overshoot or truncation. The manuscript does not clearly detail how predictions are terminated or truncated when a generated motif exceeds the target horizon.

Competitive performance against external patch-based models: While the method cleanly outperforms the matched patch-based Chronos baseline and MOMENT, Moirai still achieves lower MSE on 3 of the 5 datasets (ETTh1, Weather, Electricity in Table 3). While differences in pretraining corpus and architecture explain part of this, the comparison indicates that motif tokenization does not uniformly surpass modern patch-based foundation models.

strengths: Novel and intuitive formulation: Adapting Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) to time series after equiprobable/uniform discretization addresses a core limitation of prior discrete foundation models (like Chronos) which tokenize per-step, leading to excessively long sequences and high computational cost.

Conditional decoding is an elegant and computationally cheap post-hoc dequantization method. Solving analytically for the conditional expectation under a first-order Markov assumption provides consistent MSE reductions without requiring gradient optimization or inference overhead.

Rigorous, controlled experimental design: The authors conducted an extensive compute-heavy study (training dozens of T5 foundation models across sizes from tiny to large on the Chronos pretraining corpus) to isolate the impact of tokenization against standard single-sample and fixed patch baselines.

Thorough empirical analysis and interpretability: The submission provides rich ablations on vocabulary size, occurrence thresholds, noise and outlier robustness, as well as PCA visualizations showing that the learned embedding space organizes tokens meaningfully according to statistical moments (mean, variance) and trends.
weaknesses: Evaluation scope is limited for foundation models: While the pretraining is conducted at scale, the zero-shot evaluation is only reported on 5 classic datasets (ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather, Electricity, Traffic). Recent foundation model literature (e.g., Chronos, MOMENT, Moirai, GIFT-eval) routinely evaluates across dozens of diverse datasets from the Monash archive.

Unclear handling of prediction horizon boundaries: Because motifs have variable temporal lengths, autoregressively generating next tokens does not naturally guarantee landing exactly on a fixed target forecast horizon (e.g., exactly 64 steps). The manuscript does not clearly explain how the decoding handles overshooting or truncation at the boundary.

Potential target data leakage / deviation from pure zero-shot in conditional decoding: Section 5.3 states that conditional decoding parameters are estimated on the respective target dataset's training split to dequantize test set forecasts. While lightweight and linear, this means the results reported in Table 2 and Table 3 rely on target domain statistics, departing from a strictly zero-shot transfer protocol.

strengths: Conceptual novelty and clean formulation: Applying Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) to discretized time series provides a principled, adaptive, pattern-centric tokenization scheme that directly addresses the rigidity of fixed-length patching and the high computational cost of per-sample tokenization.

Rigorous experimental design: The authors control for confounders by comparing motif-based tokenization against Chronos baselines on identical backbones (T5 architectures across five sizes), pretraining data, and training budgets, isolating the true effect of the tokenization scheme.

Substantial empirical gains: The method achieves both large computational speedups (up to 28x-57x faster inference) and notable accuracy improvements (up to 40-48% MSE reduction over Chronos), demonstrating Pareto dominance across multiple standard zero-shot forecasting benchmarks.

Simple and effective conditional decoding: The proposed analytical conditional decoding method effectively mitigates quantization error without gradient computations or runtime inference overhead, and even exhibits benefits as a post-hoc filter on other continuous models.

Thorough analysis and interpretability: The paper includes extensive ablations on vocabulary size, occurrence threshold, quantization granularity, context length disentanglement, PCA of the embedding space, and robustness to noise, non-stationarity, and transients.
weaknesses: Focus restricted to discrete univariate generation: The BPE framework naturally targets discrete autoregressive language-model-style time series forecasters (e.g., Chronos). While univariate channel-independent modeling is standard in many foundation models, the approach does not natively accommodate joint multivariate tokenization.

Evaluation restricted to fixed prediction horizons: All zero-shot evaluations use a fixed forecast horizon of 64 time steps. It remains unexplored whether motif-based generation suffers from horizon-dependent token boundary misalignments or degradation across much longer prediction horizons (e.g., 336 or 720 steps commonly evaluated in the patch forecasting literature).

Dependency on binning heuristic: The motif extraction quality relies on the initial uniform discretization step. While the authors show uniform binning works well empirically, performance remains sensitive to the choice of the number of bins M and clipping range [omega_lb, omega_ub].

strengths: Compelling and novel adaptation of Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) to time series foundation modeling, bridging the gap between rigid fixed-length patching and inefficient point-wise tokenization.

Conditional decoding provides an elegant, computationally free closed-form dequantization mechanism (based on Markov transitions) that recovers continuous values and significantly cuts down quantization error.

Exceptionally rigorous experimental design: an apples-to-apples comparison against Chronos across five model scales (from 8M to 710M parameters) using identical architectures, pretraining datasets, and training budgets, isolating tokenization as the causal factor.

Comprehensive empirical validation across seven benchmarks (including the large-scale 37-dataset Fev-bench), demonstrating substantial zero-shot MSE improvements (up to 40-48%) and dramatic inference acceleration (over 20x).

Thorough ablation and interpretability studies, including embedding PCA (showing emergent alignment with motif mean, standard deviation, and trends), parent-child token similarity, vocabulary pruning thresholds, and robustness against noise, non-stationarity, and outliers.
weaknesses: Handling of exact prediction horizons during inference is not fully clarified: because motifs have variable lengths, autoregressive generation of discrete motif tokens will rarely sum to exactly the target horizon (e.g., exactly 64 steps), requiring truncation or post-processing that warrants explicit discussion.

In Section 5.3, the main conditional decoding results fit the dequantization parameters on the test dataset's training split, which acts as test-domain adaptation rather than a strictly zero-shot evaluation (although Appendix C.3 partially addresses a domain-independent setting).

Vocabulary construction sensitivity: BPE frequency counts are inherently dependent on the initial quantization granularity M and normalization scheme; a high M fragments recurring patterns, while a low M increases discretization error.

Comparisons to continuous multivariate foundation models (e.g., MOMENT, Moirai) are conducted under different pretraining corpora and backbones, making it harder to disentangle architecture/data effects from tokenization effects outside the Chronos family.

strengths: Novel and elegant adaptation of byte pair encoding (BPE) to time series: By pairing discretization with hierarchical BPE merging, the method creates adaptive-length temporal motifs that dynamically allocate token capacity based on pattern complexity, moving beyond rigid fixed-length patches.

Conditional decoding is a simple, effective, and practically cost-free post-hoc method: Formulating dequantization as an analytical first-order conditional expectation requires no backpropagation or runtime inference overhead, yet reliably recovers significant discretization error across various datasets and even benefits patch-based baselines.

Rigorous, controlled experimental design: The authors isolate the tokenization mechanism by training T5 architectures across five model scales under identical compute budgets, optimization hyperparameters, and training corpora against both sample-based (Chronos) and patch-based baselines.

Extensive analysis and ablation studies: The paper and appendix provide deep insights, including principal component analysis of learned motif representations (showing alignment with statistical moments and trends), sensitivity to vocabulary size and minimum occurrence threshold pmin, noise robustness, and input-length disentanglement.
weaknesses: Efficiency gains in the abstract and introduction are somewhat overstated: The headline claim of boosting efficiency by '2314 % on average' (Table 2) is obtained by comparing a smaller motif-based model (e.g., Tiny) against the best/largest Chronos baseline (e.g., Large) that it matches or outperforms. While practically useful, for iso-parameter comparisons (Table 12), the real-world inference speedup is typically around 2x to 4x.

Evaluation is restricted to a single, short prediction horizon of 64 steps: Modern long-term forecasting benchmarks commonly evaluate multiple horizons (e.g., 96, 192, 336, 720). It remains unclear how variable-length motif decoding behaves over extended horizons and how boundary alignment is handled when the horizon length is not an exact multiple of the generated motif lengths.

Context length discrepancy in the main zero-shot comparison: In Table 2, both Chronos and the proposed model receive 128 context tokens. However, because motif-based tokens compress multiple time steps, the proposed model observes substantially longer effective historical context (~384–500 time steps) than sample-based Chronos (128 time steps). Although Appendix Table 15 investigates equal sample contexts, this nuance should be clarified more prominently in the main text.
